topics.title: Fundamentals of Tries
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Fundamentals of Tries.

pages.title: Step 1 — Start Here
pages.content:
### Before you code
**Prerequisite:** Trees, strings, arrays, and references.

This topic follows a deliberate sequence. Do not skip directly to the hardest practice set.

**Your learning route**
1. Build the mental model.
2. Learn when the pattern applies.
3. Dry-run a tiny example.
4. Build the algorithm with guidance.
5. Solve a micro variation.
6. Progress through the practice ladder.
7. Pass the mastery gate.

**First question to answer:** What information must remain correct after every step of the algorithm?
pages.teachingGoal: Know the prerequisite, learning sequence, and invariant you will track.

pages.title: Step 2 — Build the Mental Model
pages.content:
### Understand before implementing
A trie stores strings by shared prefixes, making prefix-oriented queries proportional to key length rather than the number of stored words.

**Recognition rule**
Look for many prefix queries, autocomplete, dictionary matching, or shared-prefix grouping.

**Do not memorize a code template yet.** First identify what state the algorithm must maintain and what information it can safely discard.
pages.teachingGoal: Explain the idea in plain language and identify when it should be considered.

pages.title: Step 3 — Worked Dry Run
pages.content:
### Trace before code
Draw the trie for a few short words and follow one insertion/search path character by character.

Use a table with four columns:
- **Step / index**
- **Current input/state**
- **Important invariant**
- **Decision / next state**

Then test one boundary case before implementing.
pages.teachingGoal: Trace the state transition without depending on the final code.

pages.title: Step 4 — Guided Build
pages.content:
### Build it in small pieces
Choose node representation -> insert characters -> mark word termination -> traverse for search/prefix query.

**Guided order**
1. Write the inputs and outputs.
2. State the invariant.
3. Write pseudocode.
4. Implement only the first transition.
5. Test on the tiny example.
6. Add the remaining loop/recursion/structure.
7. Test an edge case.
8. State time and space complexity.

**Common trap:** Forgetting end-of-word markers, duplicate words, or allocating/visiting the wrong child.
pages.teachingGoal: Turn the mental model into a correct implementation without jumping straight to a full template.

pages.title: Need of Trie
pages.content:
Have you ever wondered how a search suggestion works, how a massive website like Google can look through billions of search strings, match them with the string typed by you and show you similar strings that might auto-complete your sentence, all in an instant. How a document editor can check the word typed by you against all the words in the dictionary in an instant to see if your spelling is correct or not?  

These operations and much more are done by a data structure called **Trie** and in this course you will learn all you need to know to implement and use tries yourself.

Operations of tries that you will learn in this course are:
- Insertion
- Search
- Deletion
- Print

### Applications of Trie
- Auto-Complete Systems
- Spell Checkers
- Prefix Matching
- Dictionary Implementations
- Text Compressions
- Genomic Sequence Analysis
- Routing Information Protocol
- Contact Management
- Word Games
- Compiler Design

options: Apply the correct algorithmic idea and handle the specified edge cases
Assume the largest possible answer is always correct

pages.title: Spell-Check MCQ
pages.content:
There exists a special dictionary with only specific words. These words are entered in a trie which is given below.
```
          [e         t]
          /         / \
        [i]       [h]  [w]
        /        /       \
      [g]      [r]       [o]
      /        /           \
    [h]     [e  o]        [end]
    /       /    \
  [t]     [e]     [n]
  /       /         \
[end]   [end]        [e]
                       \
                      [end]

```
Do the words trees and throne exist in this dictionary?

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Spell-Check MCQ and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Auto-Complete MCQ
pages.content:
Given the prefix string S = "sa", what are the string can be formed from the following trie which starts with "sa".
```
               [s]
               /
         [a______o]
        /         \
     [f______v]    [end]
     /        \
    [e]       [e]
    /           \
[[r],end]    [[d],end]
   /              \
[end]             [end]
```

topics.title: Fundamentals of DSU
topics.description: Learn fundamentals of dsu through focused explanations and DSU practice.

pages.title: Example Use Of DSU
pages.content:
Suppose there is a network of friends in a social networking site and you wanted to check if two people are connected. 



You would typically traverse the whole network containing person 1 to check if person 2 is present on the same network.\
This task can be done more efficiently without traversing the whole network with the help of a data structure called Disjoint Set Union or DSU.\
Tasks like finding connected components, finding minimum spanning tree, identifying connected components in images and checking if two components are connected in networks like social networks and computer networks can be done very efficiently using DSU.  

In this course you'll learn all you need to know about DSU.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Example Use Of DSU focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

checkpoint.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of DSU's find operation?
options: It returns the representative of the set containing an element.
It always creates a new set for the element.
It sorts every element in the data structure.
It deletes the representative of a set.
checkpoint.explanation: find follows parent links to the set representative; path compression can also shorten future searches.

pages.title: Introduction to Disjoint Set Union
pages.content:
### Disjoint Set Union  
**Disjoint Set Union** or **DSU** is a data structure used to represents a group of unique elements as part of different sets. These sets are represented by a leader element.  
**For Example**  
Assume we have 8 nodes: **0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7**  
At first they all belong to individual sets.  
```
{0}     {1}      {2}      {3}       {4}        {5}          {6}        {7}
```
If we add a connection or an edge between 1 and 3 then the sets become
```
{0}   {12->1<-3}      {5}          {6}        {7}   
```
Now there are 5 sets and the second set is identified by the leader 1.

We store a set in the form of trees with the root of the tree being the leader of the set.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Introduction to Disjoint Set Union focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Need of DSU
pages.content:
DSU is very useful when dealing with data containing elements connected with one another. 
Some common uses of DSU include:  
- Keeping track of connected components in a graph
- Detecting cycles in a graph 
- Identifying mutual friends
- Calculating the minimum spanning tree in a graph
- Checking connected components in a computer network or social network

**For example**  
   
In this graph, we have seven components. A, B, C, and D would have the same leader in a DSU and thus would be in the same set. Similarly, G and F would have the same leader and thus would be in the same set. And E will be in another set. Thus making it very easy to find connected components in a graph.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Need of DSU focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Functions in DSU
pages.content:
There are two main operations in DSU:  
- **Find** - used to find the representative or leader of the set to which the element belongs
- **Union** - used to combine two sets

These are the only two functions a DSU provides, but they can be used to solve a wide variety of problems.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Functions in DSU focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Find in DSU
pages.content:
To store the elements in a DSU, we maintain an array called **parent**. The **parent** array holds the value of parent element for each element. If the element has no parent, it is saved as its own parent. At the beginning, when the graph has no edges or connections every element is its own parent.

The below set of elements will be represented like this in the parent array:  
0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3  
4  
5

Parent array => [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5]

The parent of 0 is 1, 1 is 2, 2 is 3 and 3 is 3 itself. Same for 4 and 5.

In a DSU each set is represented by the leader (or the element with no parent). To find the leader of a set we recursively go to the parent of the current element until we reach an element which is its own parent. Then we return that element. Read the pseudo-code for better understanding 

#### Pseudo-Code
```python
function find(element){
    if (parent[element] == element) 
        return element
    else
        return find(parent[element])
}
```

#### Dry-Run
Let's assume we have a DSU having the following set:
```
     0
   /   \
  1     2
 /
3
```
This will have the following parent array $P$ = [0, 0, 0, 1].  
Here the ${P_i}$ is the parent of index $i$.
If we call find(3), it will run in following steps.
- parent[3] is 1 which is not equal to 3, so we call find(1).
- parent[1] is 0 which is not equal to 1, so we call find(0).
- parent[0] is 0 which equal to 0, so we return 0.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Find in DSU focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Union in DSU
pages.content:
Union operation is used to join two sets into a single set.

We first check if the elements are already in the same set. This can be checked by performing find on both elements and comparing their results. If they have the same leader, we don't have to do anything as they are already in the same set. Otherwise, we set the one set's leader as the parent of another set's leader. Read the pseudo code for better understanding

```python
function union(a, b) {
    leader_a = find(a)
    leader_b = find(b)
    if(leader_a != leader_b){
        parent[leader_b] = leader_a
    }
}
```

#### Dry-Run ####
Let's assume we have a DSU having the following sets:
```
     0
   /   \
  1     2
 /
3
     4
   /   \
  5     6
```
This will have the following parent array $P$ = [0, 0, 0, 1, 4, 4, 4].  
Here the ${P_i}$ is the parent of index $i$.  
If we call union(3, 5), it will run in following steps.
- leader_a will be set to the value returned by find(3) which will be 0.
- leader_b will be set to the value returned by find(5) which will be 4.
- Since leader_a and leader_b are not equal they currently do not belong to the same group.
- So we set parent[leader_a] equal to leader_b
- Thus the new sets will look like this:
```
     0
   / | \
  1  2  4
 /     /  \
3     5    6
```

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Union in DSU focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Time Complexity of Naive DSU implementation
pages.content:
In the basic implementation, in worst case, nodes can form long chains. For example:  
1 <- 2 <- 3 <- 4 <- 5 <- 6 <- 7 <- 8 <- 9  
For 9, the dsuFind function will have to traverse through all the nodes to find the leader. Making the worst case time complexity $O(N)$.  
  
We can greatly improve this and make it more efficient by applying some heuristics to avoid long chains from forming.  

Through these optimizations, we can achieve a time complexity of almost $O(1)$ (the worst-case time complexity of O($\alpha$(n)) where $\alpha$(n) is inverse Ackermann function which grows very slowly. In fact it grows so slowly, that it doesn't exceed $4$  for all reasonable $n$.).

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Time Complexity of Naive DSU implementation focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Optimization 1 - Find
pages.content:
### Optimization 1 - Path Compression 
When we call find(v) for a vertex v to find the leader of the set v belongs to, we call find(v). Find(v) goes through all the vertices between **v** and the leader.

If we save the leader in this process, then next time when we need to call find(u) for any vertex in the path from **v** to leader, we can directly return the leader.  

## Pseudo-code
```python
function find(element) {
    if (parent[element] == element) 
    {
        return element
    }
    else
    {
        leader_element = find(parent[element])
        # The optimization step to store the leader as parent for each node
        parent[element] = leader_element
        return leader_element
    }
}
```
In this code all that's changed is that we update the parent of the element to the leader of the set before returning the leader.  
## For Example  
In the set  
```
      3
     /  
    4
   /  
  5
 /
6
```
When we call find(6), the following steps occur:
- find(6) calls find(5)
- find(4) calls find(4)
- find(4) calls find(3)
- 3 is the parent of itself so it is the leader, so it returns itself.
- At find(4) before returning 3 it sets the parent of 4 as 3 which is already the case.
- At find(5) before returning 3 it sets the parent of 5 as 3.
- At find(6) before returning 3 it sets the parent of 6 as 3.
Now the updated set is
```
  3
 /|\
4 5 6
```
Thus next time we can find the leader in just one or two operations.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Optimization 1 - Find focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.

pages.title: Optimization 2 - Union
pages.content:
In our current implementation when we perform union the second tree always gets attached to the first one. This can again lead to long chains.  

### Example 
Suppose we have following operation: **union(1, 2)**  
This creates the tree: 11 1 <--2  
     ^
     |
     4
```

This heuristic helped us in improving the complexity by changing the leader of as few nodes as possible in each **union** operation.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Optimization 2 - Union focuses on a concrete DSU technique: maintaining representatives, merging sets, or exploiting DSU efficiency.
